claims.text: In situ aberration-corrected TEM can detect thermally induced structural changes at atomic scale in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a random, disordered atomic arrangement.
Controlled thermal annealing can be performed using an in situ heating stage in an aberration-corrected TEM.
Gradual heating can capture the onset of diffusion-driven structural modifications.
Thermally activated atomic diffusion can produce local atomic rearrangement in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermally activated diffusion can produce minor atomic ordering.
Thermally activated diffusion can produce phase separation.
Increasing temperature raises atomic mobility relative to room temperature.
Atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles is sluggish at room temperature.
Heating may cause ordered clusters to form.
Heating may cause segregation into compositionally distinct phases.
In situ TEM can directly track these rearrangements at atomic scale.
Above a transformation threshold, ordered regions or nanoscale compositional inhomogeneities are expected relative to the room-temperature state.
Before heating, the room-temperature baseline is homogeneous and disordered.
Below a critical temperature, no significant atomic rearrangement occurs.
Above the critical temperature, detectable changes in local order or phase occur.
Nanoparticle size, local composition variation, and energetic barriers affect the onset and extent of transformation.
SAED and EELS/EDS measurements can respectively identify phase changes and compositional segregation during heating.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule treats a lack of observed change over an unspecified thermal regime as decisive, although the boundary requires crossing an unknown critical temperature and the uncertainty field states that the transformation onset is not predicted. Failure to observe a transformation therefore would not necessarily falsify the claimed capability of AC-TEM.
